Former Kaduna Central senator Shehu Sani has identified eight factors contributing to growing political and social divisions between Nigeria’s North and the Middle Belt.
The North-central region and parts of the North-west and North-east, largely occupied by non-Muslim minority ethnic groups, are considered the Middle Belt.
Mr Sani listed the factors in a social media post in which he called for an intelligent debate on what he described as the political drift between the two parts of northern Nigeria.
The factors include decades of ethno-religious conflicts, banditry and terrorist attacks, divisive statements by some northern leaders, perceived marginalisation of ethnic minorities and what he described as a superiority complex among majority groups.
He also cited alleged external influence, foreign interference and hostile exchanges between young people from the two areas on social media.
Mr Sani said the divisions had been reinforced by religious and ethnic differences, as well as political and social tensions.
His intervention comes amid renewed discussions about the relationship between the core North and the Middle Belt, particularly over political representation, security and the treatment of ethnic minorities.

Mr Sani’s post attracted responses from Nigerians, some of whom argued that the divisions were rooted in political exclusion and unequal power relations.
Joe Rindap said the North-central was often recognised as part of the North when discussions centred on population but was excluded from political calculations, particularly power-sharing arrangements.
He argued that the Middle Belt should unite to resist what he described as manipulation and oppression by the core North.
Similarly, Ayuba Doekyil said the issue goes beyond religion and has a significant political dimension.
He argued that people in the North-central had for years felt marginalised within the broader northern political structure, particularly in decisions concerning power-sharing and key political appointments.
Mr Doekyil said the Middle Belt was often expected to identify with the North without being treated as an equal partner.
He maintained that lasting unity would require mutual respect, fairness and political inclusion.
However, Mustapha Abubakar disagreed with the suggestion that the North and Middle Belt were drifting apart because of the factors listed by Mr Sani.
He argued that ethno-religious conflicts and insecurity were not peculiar to the North or the Middle Belt, noting that other parts of Nigeria had experienced similar communal disputes.
On insecurity, Mr Abubakar said banditry and terrorism had affected states in the core North, including Zamfara, Sokoto, Katsina, Kaduna and Kebbi, where Muslim communities had also suffered attacks.
He also challenged the claim of systematic marginalisation, arguing that people from the North-central had occupied prominent political and public offices, including positions as Senate presidents, speakers, governors, ministers and service chiefs since 1999.
Mr Abubakar said political actors on both sides had made divisive statements and warned against allowing politicians and social media exchanges to deepen divisions.
He further argued that communities across the region continued to maintain social and economic relationships despite the hostility expressed online.
Lukman Gumi also cautioned against allowing religious and ethnic differences to define relationships between the two areas.
He said both regions have more interests in common than differences and urged Nigerians to focus on demanding security, justice and good leadership.
Mr Sani’s call for debate also comes days after he criticised what he described as the lack of public outrage over an attack on worshippers in Zamfara State .
In a Facebook post on Sunday, 15 November, he questioned why Nigerians were not more vocal in condemning the attack on a mosque in Kaura town, Kaura Namoda Local Government Area, where suspected bandits reportedly killed one worshipper and abducted several others.
According to ARISE News in a report published on 16 November, the former senator questioned the silence surrounding the incident and challenged Nigerians to condemn bandits and terrorists regardless of their religious identity.
“Why is it that no one is condemning or cursing the bandits for their genocide? Why is it that everyone is ignoring this story?” he asked.
He also questioned the religious identity of the attackers, asking: “What is the religion of these bandits if they have any?”
Mr Sani further asked whether Nigerians had run out of anger or tears over the persistent violence.
“Can we now begin to reason that bandits and terrorists are common evils to us all?” he added.
The comments reflect his broader appeal for Nigerians to avoid viewing insecurity through religious divisions and to recognise armed groups as a common threat.
Mr Sani, who represented Kaduna Central in the Senate from 2015 to 2019, is seeking a return to the National Assembly in 2027. He recently won the All Progressives Congress (APC) senatorial primary for Kaduna Central, according to reports on the party’s selection process.
